items.title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents
items.summary: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.

items.title: $μ$-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Interaction Voice Agents
items.summary: Voice agents in shared spaces must satisfy interdependent multi-user requests while upholding per-user authority, privacy, and task constraints. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage when participants react throughout a session. We introduce $μ$-Bench, a benchmark for joint task completion in closed-loop, full-duplex multi-user voice interaction. Simulated participants act from isolated profiles of goals, knowledge, and permissions, adapting to the agent's speech and tool outcomes. Across 20 domains, 100 scenarios vary group size, acoustics, and follow-up demands to form 800 cases (408 tool-augmented, 392 tool-free). Joint Task Success (JTS) requires all user goals, privacy boundaries, and terminal states to hold jointly, while Pure JTS further disallows unauthorized tool calls; Attribution, Threading, and Coordination (ATC) diagnostics localize failures. Across 13 voice agents, proprietary systems peak at 62.24\% tool-free and 65.44\% tool-augmented success, while open-weight models remain below 20\%. ATC diagnostics show that open-weight models lag primarily in multi-turn attribution and threading, and controlled contrasts reveal that larger groups consistently degrade joint task success across capable systems. By coupling reactive multi-user simulation with verifiable session-level outcomes, $μ$-Bench provides a rigorous testbed for shared voice agents.

items.title: How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? An Empirical Study of Unneeded Edits in Repository-Level Agent Patches
items.summary: Agent patches are larger than developers', which is widely read as over-editing. But patch size does not say whether the extra edits are needed, what they are, or where they come from. We introduce Delta Residue Attribution (DRA), which replays agent trajectories, traces every block (unit) of the final patch to the step that wrote it, reverts each unit, and reruns the task tests to decide whether the unit is needed. We apply DRA to 7,660 resolved GitHub Copilot CLI trajectories from 18 frontier models on SWE-bench Verified (6,728) and DeepSWE (932), and grade developer patches using the same method. Agent patches do change more lines than developers'; on SWE-bench Verified the majority of extra edits add tests (61%) and documentation (13%) while on DeepSWE, most extra edits are code (58%). On both benchmarks, agents' code is on average at least as necessary as developers' (mean $NP_{code}$ 0.887 vs. 0.864 on SWE-bench Verified, where 11 of 18 models leave less unneeded code than developers, and 0.797 vs. 0.785 on DeepSWE). On average, 11% of an agent patch's code units on SWE-bench Verified are still unneeded, and 89% of those change behavior. Debug steps write almost none of the unneeded code. Code necessity differs substantially by model; it is unrelated to resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified and negatively correlated with it on DeepSWE (Spearman -0.59, p = 0.01). On SWE-bench Verified, pruning with DRA using only the tests the agent can see (its own tests and the repository's) removes the majority of unneeded code but also some needed code (67% recall, 46% precision), and 89% of pruned patches still resolve the task; asking the agent to audit its own diff is more precise but less effective (36% recall, 66% precision). We recommend that benchmarks report code necessity next to resolve rate and that over-editing be addressed through model training and harness-level pruning.

Most agentic benchmarks only measure a single domain like coding or legal. The few that try to be comprehensive, like GDPVal or Agent’s Last Exam , make the mistake of selecting domains based on percentage of GDP or the O*NET taxonomy. AI’s impact is nowhere near evenly distributed across the economy today, and we expect this trend to intensify in the future. Many tasks already can’t justify paying for Fable 5.2, much less Fable 7. Thus, if your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they will be most impactful. It’s for this reason that GDPx intentionally forgoes industries like government and real estate, and instead covers the following domains: Our methodology is also unique. To ensure all our tasks are truly representative of their respective domains, we partnered with 14 specialized data partners to make 206 tasks. items.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
items.summary:
I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months.

Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply.

Coding agents in November 2025

Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model.

In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said:

Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.

This held up.

Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025.

Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant.

The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself.

Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks.

The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work.

Fable class models in June/July

We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them.

In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work.

After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st.

For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models. My definition of these:

In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug.

A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm.

Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook.

I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well.

These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model.

3D modeling and game development in September/October

Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for.

I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example.

3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa.

Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game. It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play.

I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play!

Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked. My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay.

Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time.

Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games.

The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster.

It feels like another inflection point to me.

Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too?

I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement.

I'm getting so much done with that model right now!

It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42, 1.0a43, and 1.0a44 - plus LLM 0.37, 0.37.1, 0.37.2, 0.37.3, and 0.38 - all in the last three weeks, represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements.

If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it. That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks.

Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don't think I'll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand.

items.story_key: model:claude|title:how the claude code team thinks about verification
items.content_excerpt: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes. If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. The interesting part is that a Claude session anywhere, from chat to Claude Code, can open the same doc and read, write, and comment in it live, right next to you. We released Docs on September 16, 2026. This post is about the service that runs underneath it. Three weeks before Claude Docs opened to the public, it was running as a proof of concept on a single node, used by a few thousand people inside Anthropic. We were racing toward an ambitious launch date, and our own estimate said we'd see millions of docs within the first few days. We launched on September 16. By September 22, people had created over 4.6 million docs. Across 2 billion requests we saw only 60 server errors, and we never had to roll back. The whole Docs service ran on about 50 memory-optimized pods. But honestly, this only worked because our frontier models have gotten much better recently (I used an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.2). In our experience, they can now stick with one goal through a run like this for weeks, which is what helped us hit launch scale in a tight timeline. A few thousand internal users on one machine told us nothing about whether the service would survive launch, and we obviously didn't have launch traffic to test with. We wanted real evidence to decide how fast we could roll out. So on September 4, about two weeks before launch, I had Claude drive a staging cluster that mirrored production at over a million synthetic docs a day and break core components on purpose. And then... I just left it running (I've included the full cost at the end of this article). My setup was pretty simple. items.title: Solve Vision with Code: Coding Agents Are Stronger Visual Reasoners Than Video Models
items.summary: Video generation models are increasingly evaluated as visual reasoners: given a first frame and a natural-language prompt, can the model produce the video in which the specified task is carried out? The paradigm is considered advantageous because the reasoning is native to the visual medium, unfolding directly in the frames rather than through language or code. Whether this native route is in fact the more reliable path to visual reasoning has not been tested against a symbolic alternative under the same conditions. We therefore pose the same tasks, with identical inputs, output specification and evaluator, to both media: rather than denoising pixels, a coding agent writes a program that renders the answer video, which an unmodified rule-based evaluator scores. On VBVR-Pro-Bench (Xu et al., 2026), a 500-instance suite spanning five cognitive categories with symbolic ground truth, the agent receives the same first frame and prompt as the video model, with no access to ground truth, metadata or generation models, and one attempt per instance. Three closed-model agents (Codex with gpt-6-astra, Claude Code with Fable 5.1 and Gemini CLI with Gemini 3.1 Pro) score 0.923, 0.894 and 0.893, each more than 0.22 above the strongest video model. Among 23 runnable open-weight models, the best, GLM-5, reaches 0.572, above all video models except the RL-trained one. Together, we show that for tasks whose solutions can be computed from a first frame and a prompt, program synthesis is currently a substantially more reliable route to visual reasoning than video generation. We further distinguish depictive programs, which navigate the image to recover a transferable scheme, from propositional programs, which operate on hard-coded values, revealing how visual reasoning unfolds in agent-written programs and what it implies for its nature of reasoning in general.

items.title: Maco-RL: Scaling Agent Capabilities with Mixed-Task Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Mixed-task reinforcement learning (MixRL) directly trains a unified policy across domains to continually expand agent capabilities without training separate specialists or requiring an extra distillation stage. Despite its appeal, scaling MixRL poses significant challenges in achieving stable and efficient mixed-task learning, effectively allocating rollout compute, and supporting continual domain expansion. To address these challenges, we propose Maco-RL, an approach that effectively scales MixRL. Specifically, Maco-RL employs a quota-based scheduler for asynchronous rollouts across multiple task domains, thereby stabilizing training by balancing gradient contributions and mitigating off-policy effects. Along an orthogonal axis, Maco-RL further introduces Tri-Buffer Sampling (TBS) to allocate compute among samples with varying levels of mastery, promoting sustained frontier exploration while preserving acquired capabilities. Experiments on five benchmarks show Maco-RL raises Qwen3.5-27B's overall score from 43.6 to 54.2 and then to 60.1 with continual expansion, reaching the frontier held by Qwen3.8-27B, which is further pushed outward by +5.7. Maco-RL also outperforms single-task RL with less compute for policy updates. These results support MixRL as a practical and compute-efficient post-training approach with substantial potential to strengthen general agent capabilities.

items.title: Data + AI Anywhere: AlloyDB Omni integration with local models
items.summary:
Open models like Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind are a great option to keep your data local. But how can a local AI model integrate with on-premises data?

AlloyDB Omni, Google’s 100% PostgreSQL-compatible database that runs anywhere, now integrates with locally hosted large language models (LLMs). With AlloyDB Omni, you can build agentic experiences on your own infrastructure and on your own terms. Whether it’s in the cloud, in your datacenter, or even on your laptop, you can have data plus AI anywhere.

Built-in AI for your local environment

AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, run-anywhere edition of AlloyDB that easily deploys to your own infrastructure, including on-premises. AlloyDB Omni packs powerful, built-in AI, including the same ScaNN indexing technology powering Google Search. When you pair AlloyDB Omni with a model, you can store vector embeddings at scale; search them semantically; and even query the database using natural language. You can use virtually any model you like, whether that’s a frontier Cloud-hosted model like Gemini or a local model. And with locally hosted models you maintain complete control over your data environment.

Connecting to Gemma 4, Qwen3.8, and other local models

You can now connect AlloyDB Omni to local models like Gemma 4 and Qwen3.8. No matter which model you choose, the architecture remains the same.

This setup enables entirely new use cases for environments that were previously blocked from adopting agentic capabilities. If you operate an air-gapped network or have data locality requirements, you can still build intelligent applications. You can analyze local logs, generate summaries of proprietary internal documents, and power localized chatbots—all while maintaining strict data governance.

  • Keep data on-premises: Because the database and the model sit in the same local environment, your data never crosses the public internet.

  • Reduce latency: Processing inference requests locally minimizes network transit time.

  • Query directly via SQL: Your standard database queries can invoke machine learning functions that process data locally. Like this:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SELECT customer_name, ai.generate('Summarize in 1 short sentence: ' || comment, model_id => 'gemma4_llm') AS summary FROM customer_feedback; customer_name | summary ---------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------- Alice | The customer demands a refund for a double charge or they will cancel Bob | The user likes the product but requests dark mode support."), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fde5b6b2710>)])]>

Next, you’ll see how to run queries like this yourself, step by step.

Get started

You can test this integration on your own machines today. Using a Kubernetes environment we will show you how to deploy and integrate AlloyDB Omni and a local open model.

Step 0: Before you begin

In this example, we will use Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to host the AlloyDB Omni database and local model. GKE gives us a standardized, reproducible environment but you can use the same setup on-prem or almost anywhere.

We will assume you have already setup:

  1. A GKE cluster, and

  2. Kubernetes tools kubectl and Helm

Step 1: Deploy the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes Operator

We will use the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes operator to set up our AlloyDB Omni database. The Operator makes deploying and maintaining AlloyDB Omni a breeze.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "helm install \ cert-manager oci://quay.io/jetstack/charts/cert-manager \ --version v1.21.3 \ --namespace cert-manager \ --create-namespace \ --set crds.enabled=true \ --set global.leaderElection.namespace=cert-manager helm install alloydbomni-operator oci://gcr.io/alloydb-omni/alloydbomni-operator \ --version 1.9.0 \ --create-namespace \ --namespace alloydb-omni-system \ $(helm install --help | grep -q -- '--rollback-on-failure' && echo '--rollback-on-failure' || echo '--atomic') \ --timeout 5m"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fde5b6b2c50>)])]>

Step 2: Create your AlloyDB Omni database

Don’t forget to enable the googleMLExtension.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'kubectl create namespace ai-demo cat << \'EOF\' | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: db-pw-my-omni namespace: ai-demo type: Opaque data: my-omni: "VmVyeVN0cm9uZ1Bhc3N3b3Jk" # password "VeryStrongPassword" --- apiVersion: alloydbomni.dbadmin.goog/v1 kind: DBCluster metadata: name: my-omni namespace: ai-demo spec: databaseVersion: "18.4.0" primarySpec: adminUser: passwordRef: name: db-pw-my-omni features: googleMLExtension: enabled: true resources: cpu: 2 memory: 4Gi disks: - name: DataDisk size: 20Gi storageClass: standard dbLoadBalancerOptions: annotations: networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "internal" allowExternalIncomingTraffic: true EOF'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fde5b6b3810>)])]>

Step 3: Deploy your AI model

We will use Ollama to help us deploy our model.

In this example we deploy Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind. Or, you can modify this command to deploy Qwen3.8 – just change a few lines as noted in the comments.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'cat << \'EOF\' | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: ollama namespace: ai-demo spec: replicas: 1 selector: matchLabels: app: ollama template: metadata: labels: app: ollama spec: containers: - name: ollama image: ollama/ollama:latest ports: - containerPort: 11434 env: - name: OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE value: "-1" # keep the model in RAM - name: OLLAMA_LOAD_TIMEOUT value: "20m" resources: requests: cpu: "4" memory: "16Gi" # for Qwen 3.8: 24Gi volumeMounts: - name: models mountPath: /root/.ollama lifecycle: postStart: exec: command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "(sleep 5 && ollama pull gemma4:12b) >/dev/null 2>&1 &"] # For Qwen 3.8, comment out the line above and use this one: # command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "(sleep 5 && ollama pull qwen3.8) >/dev/null 2>&1 &"] volumes: - name: models ephemeral: volumeClaimTemplate: spec: accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"] resources: requests: storage: 30Gi --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: ollama-service namespace: ai-demo spec: type: ClusterIP ports: - port: 11434 targetPort: 11434 selector: app: ollama EOF'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fde5b35a010>)])]>

Step 4: Register the model with AlloyDB Omni

Connect to your database.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'kubectl exec -it -n ai-demo $(kubectl get pod -n ai-demo -l alloydbomni.internal.dbadmin.goog/task-type=database -o jsonpath=\'{.items[0].metadata.name}\') -c database -- env PGPASSWORD="VeryStrongPassword" psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fde5b4106d0>)])]>

Note: If you receive a connection error, you might need to wait a moment for your database to provision.

Now you should be connected to your AlloyDB Omni database with the psql client. Next, run the following SQL script to register your local model.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS google_ml_integration; ALTER SYSTEM SET google_ml_integration.request_timeout_in_seconds = 600; SELECT pg_reload_conf(); CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION google_ml.ollama_llm_input_transform( model_id character varying, prompt text, generation_config json, system_instructions json ) RETURNS json AS $$ SELECT json_build_object( 'model', CASE model_id WHEN 'gemma4_llm' THEN 'gemma4:12b' WHEN 'qwen3_8_llm' THEN 'qwen3.8' END, 'messages', json_build_array( json_build_object('role', 'system', 'content', COALESCE(system_instructions->'systemInstruction'->'parts'->0->>'text', 'You are a helpful assistant.')), json_build_object('role', 'user', 'content', prompt) ) ); $$ LANGUAGE sql; CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION google_ml.ollama_llm_output_transform( model_id character varying, response json ) RETURNS text AS $$ SELECT trim(regexp_replace( response->'choices'->0->'message'->>'content', '<think>.*?</think>', '', 's')); $$ LANGUAGE sql; CALL google_ml.create_model( model_id => 'gemma4_llm', -- and/or 'qwen3_8_llm', model_request_url => 'http://ollama-service.ai-demo.svc.cluster.local:11434/v1/chat/completions', model_provider => 'custom', model_type => 'llm', model_in_transform_fn => 'google_ml.ollama_llm_input_transform', model_out_transform_fn => 'google_ml.ollama_llm_output_transform' );"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fde5b5a4890>)])]>

Note: If you receive a Resource not found error, wait a moment for the model to load.

In addition to registering your model, the above script tells AlloyDB Omni how to interpret the model’s raw output. In this example chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is part of the response inside <think></think> tags. We don’t want the CoT, so our output transform function removes it.

Step 5: Try it out!

You can use functions like ai.generate built-in to AlloyDB Omni to connect to your local model – without ever leaving the SQL client!

Please refund $49 immediately or I will cancel.'), ('Bob', 'Great product, but can you please add dark mode support?'); SELECT customer_name, ai.generate('Summarize in 1 short sentence: ' || comment, model_id => 'gemma4_llm' /* or 'qwen3_8_llm' */) AS summary FROM customer_feedback;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fde5b5a6d50>)])]>

Make it your own

Try out all the AI features that AlloyDB Omni has to offer! AlloyDB Omni supports fast vector search, built-in AI functions, and more. Give them a try and build something great.

items.title: Release 2.75.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.11
items.summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • PyTorch backend: Added AOTI BF16 input/output support.
  • THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt is now included in the containers.
  • Fixed a use-after-free in the dynamic batcher and a preserve_ordering completion-slot issue on response-cache hits.
  • Prevented silent gRPC stream cancellations under backpressure.
  • Bounded the decompressed HTTP inference response size in the client library.
  • Perf Analyzer: Honored supplied output shapes, propagated the binary exit code, tagged the wheel as platform-specific, and limited profile-data export to the needed inputs and outputs.
  • Python backend: Now logs when the backend stub exits on a crash signal.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
